explanations.explanation: Rome it is. Paul says, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) The man hasn't even left for Jerusalem yet and he's already penciling in the next city. I can't plan past tomorrow's batch, so I'm impressed.
Athens is a good guess, friend, but it's not the city Paul names here. He says, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) Rome is the city he names after Jerusalem.
Antioch is a good guess, but Paul doesn't name it in this verse. After Jerusalem, he says, "I must see Rome as well." (Acts 19:21) That's a big jump on the map, and he's already looking at it.

explanations.answer: He stays behind for a time
explanations.explanation: That's right. Timothy and Erastus go ahead to Macedonia, while Paul "…stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy is one of Paul's helpers, and so is Erastus. Paul sends them off, and he stays put for a time.

Not yet, friend. Paul has Jerusalem in his plans (Acts 19:21), but this verse says he stayed for a time in the province of Asia. At this point in the passage, Jerusalem is only what he has resolved to do. Hold your horses, baker.

Close, but it's the other way around. Paul sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia, "…while he stayed for a time in the province of Asia." (Acts 19:22) Timothy and Erastus are his two helpers. They go on ahead, and Paul stays put for a while.
Business is the word. The silver shrines of Artemis bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is the silversmith who makes them. The text says much business, not a little.

I like the sunny thinking, friend, but the text says something more down to earth. The shrines bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Money is what's on the line here, and you'll see why that matters in a minute.

Fame sounds fancy, but that's not the word. The verse says the shrines bring "…much business to the craftsmen." (Acts 19:24) Demetrius is a silversmith who makes them. It's business the verse names, not fame.

Paul, the apostle, is the man. Demetrius says, "…this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) Notice he says it to the craftsmen, who make their living from those shrines. He's got their full attention.
Apollos isn't the name Demetrius gives here. He says, "…this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26) Paul is the one in the crosshairs of this meeting.

Silas is a fun name to throw out, friend, but Demetrius never says it. He has gathered the craftsmen and the workmen in related trades (Acts 19:25). He points at just one man and says, "…this Paul has persuaded a great number of people to turn away." (Acts 19:26)

True. Demetrius says of Paul, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) That's Demetrius describing Paul's message to the craftsmen and the workmen in related trades he gathered (Acts 19:25). I bet that message did not go over well with people whose business was shrines.

It's actually true, friend. Demetrius says, "He says that man-made gods are no gods at all." (Acts 19:26) He's telling the craftsmen what he's heard Paul say. A shrine maker would not enjoy hearing that line.

True. Demetrius warns that "…the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed…" (Acts 19:27) So he's worried about more than his own paycheck. He brings the temple into it too.
It's true, friend. Demetrius says there's danger "…that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited and her majesty deposed…" (Acts 19:27) He adds the temple to the business worries.

Shouting it is. "When the men heard this, they were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:28) Demetrius finished talking, and the volume went straight up. Their first move after hearing him is to shout.
That's a calm idea, and these men are anything but calm. The text says they "…were enraged and began shouting…" (Acts 19:28) Closing shops isn't what the verse says they do. Shouting is.

Good guess, but it isn't what the text says. They "…were enraged and began shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:28) The shouting comes first, and going after Paul isn't in this verse. The next verse shows the whole city in disarray.

Right, those are the two. The crowd rushed into the theatre, "…dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Imagine just trying to travel with a friend and getting pulled into this.

Those two are Paul's helpers, and Paul sent them ahead to Macedonia (Acts 19:22). But the crowd drags into the theatre "…Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Those are the two names the verse gives.

Not this time, friend. The crowd drags in "…Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s traveling companions from Macedonia." (Acts 19:29) Paul isn't in the theatre. The next verses tell you he wanted to be, though.

Not quite. The text says, "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) So Paul wanted to go, and the disciples said no. I think they were looking out for him.

False is right. "Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples would not allow him." (Acts 19:30) The disciples did not allow him to go before the assembly. I think that was a good friend move.

explanations.answer: Officials of the province of Asia
explanations.explanation: Yes, officials of the province of Asia. "Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) They didn't just ask, they begged. These are friends of Paul who hold office in the province.

The text doesn't name synagogue leaders here. It says, "Even some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre." (Acts 19:31) These friends hold office in the province.
Soldiers aren't mentioned in this verse. The ones who send word are "…some of Paul’s friends who were officials of the province of Asia…" (Acts 19:31) They begged him to stay out of the theatre.

Not at all, friend. The text says "…most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) Some were shouting one thing and some another. That means most of the people in the theatre didn't know the reason they were there.

False is right. "Some were shouting one thing and some another, and most of them did not even know why they were there." (Acts 19:32) That says most of them, not every last person. A lot of people shouting, and most of them not knowing why.

That's it. Alexander "…motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) He's the man the Jews in the crowd pushed forward. He gets his hand up first and plans to talk next.

No bowing in this passage, friend. Alexander "…motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) The Jews in the crowd had just pushed him forward. Pushed to the front of a loud crowd, and the first thing he asks for is quiet. I think that takes nerve.

No scroll in this scene, friend. Alexander "…motioned for silence so he could make his defense to the people." (Acts 19:33) The crowd had pushed him forward, and the first thing he does is signal for quiet.

explanations.answer: They all shout over him together
explanations.explanation: That's right. Alexander motions for silence so he can make his defense (Acts 19:33). Then "…when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:34) The verse records two hours of the same shout.

explanations.answer: They let him finish his defense
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says "…when they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted in unison for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”" (Acts 19:34) Alexander had motioned for silence to make his defense (Acts 19:33). The verse records two hours of shouting.

explanations.answer: They carry him out of the theatre
explanations.explanation: Nothing about carrying him out here. When they realized he was a Jew, "…they all shouted in unison for about two hours…" (Acts 19:34) The crowd answered with noise, not with a carry-out.

True. After the city clerk quieted the crowd, he declared, "…doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?" (Acts 19:35) He's reminding them of something he says everyone knows. The quieting comes first, and then he speaks.

It's true, friend. The city clerk says, "…doesn’t everyone know that the city of Ephesus is guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven?" (Acts 19:35) He's the one who finally got the crowd quiet.

It's the other way around. The clerk says, "…you have brought these men here, though they have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess." (Acts 19:37) So the men they dragged in did neither of those things.
False is right. The clerk says the men "…have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess." (Acts 19:37) That's a clear statement from the city clerk, in front of the whole crowd.

The courts are right. The clerk says, "…the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. That's where he points Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen if they have a complaint.

The clerk doesn't send them to the temple. He says, "…the courts are open and proconsuls are available. Let them bring charges against one another there." (Acts 19:38) A proconsul is a Roman governor. Complaints go to the courts.
The synagogue isn't mentioned in the clerk's speech. He says, "…the courts are open and proconsuls are available." (Acts 19:38) That's where complaints belong, he says.
Legal is the word. The clerk says, "…it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) A proper meeting with proper rules, not a theatre full of people shouting different things.
Sacred sounds right for a crowd shouting about a temple, but that's not the word. The clerk says, "…it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) He's pointing them to the proper process.

Secret would be a surprise, friend. The clerk says, "…it must be settled in a legal assembly." (Acts 19:39) Legal is the word he uses, and secret never shows up. That's where he says anything beyond the courts must go.

Rioting is the word. The clerk says, "…we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events…" (Acts 19:40) He says "we," so he counts himself in. I think he's telling them to calm down before it gets worse.

The charge isn't theft. In fact, the clerk says the men they dragged in did not rob the temple (Acts 19:37). He warns, "…we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events…" (Acts 19:40)

Treason sounds heavier, friend, but the clerk never says it. He says, "…we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events…" (Acts 19:40) Notice the "we," so he counts himself in on the jeopardy. I think that's one worried clerk.

That's right. "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) First the clerk quieted the crowd (Acts 19:35). Then he spoke, and then he dismissed them. Before that, they had shouted for about two hours (Acts 19:34).
No arrest in this passage. The text says, "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) The clerk had pointed Demetrius and the craftsmen to the courts instead.

Nope, friend. The disciples would not allow Paul to go before the assembly (Acts 19:30), and his friends who were officials begged him not to venture into the theatre (Acts 19:31). After the clerk's speech, "…he dismissed the assembly." (Acts 19:41) Nobody sends for Paul in this passage.
